title: Retries, timeouts and model fallback for OpenAI-compatible APIs in ~40 lines of Python
author: lucky wang
summary: Disclosure: I work on the APIGOTO team. APIGOTO is an independent OpenAI-compatible API gateway and is not affiliated with OpenAI, Anthropic or Google. The pattern below works with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, ours or not. When a prototype calls an LLM API, the first production problem is rarely the prompt. It's a 429, a slow response that hangs your worker, or one model being temporarily unavailable. Here is the small wrapper I use to handle all three. The idea Set a hard timeout on every request. Retry rate-limit and server errors with exponential backoff. If a model keeps failing, move on to the next model in a list. Code import os , time from openai import OpenAI , APIStatusError , APITimeoutError , APIConnectionError client = OpenAI ( base_url = os . getenv ( " LLM_BASE_URL " , " https://api.china-aiapi.com/v1 " ), api_key = os . environ [ " LLM_API_KEY " ], timeout = 30 , # never wait forever max_retries = 0 , # we handle retries ourselves ) RETRYABLE = { 429 , 500 , 502 , 503 , 504 } def chat ( messages , models , attempts = 3 ): last_err = None for model in models : for i in range ( attempts ): try : r = client . chat . completions . create ( model = model , messages = messages ) return model , r . choices [ 0 ]. message . content except APIStatusError as e : last_err = e if e . status_code not in RETRYABLE : break # 400/401/404: retrying won't help, try next model except ( APITimeoutError , APIConnectionError ) as e : last_err = e time . sleep ( min ( 2 ** i , 8 )) raise RuntimeError ( f " all models failed: { last_err } " ) model , text = chat ( [{ " role " : " user " , " content " : " Summarize HTTP 429 in one sentence. " }], models = [ " your-primary-model " , " your-backup-model " ], ) print ( model , text ) Notes Use the model IDs your provider actually lists ( client.models.list() ), not names you assume exist. A 401 or 404 means fix your key or model name; don't retry it. Log which model answered. When the fallback fires often, you want to know. Because only base_url and the key change, you can point this at OpenAI directly, a self-hosted server, or a gateway. If you want to try it against our gateway, the base URL is https://api.china-aiapi.com/v1 , and pricing is pay-as-you-go: www.china-aiapi.com . Feedback on the pattern is welcome in the comments.

title: How to search the Internet Archive from Python and get direct download links
author: Gio Rich
summary: I built this actor; it's a paid tool on Apify with a free trial credit. The Internet Archive holds millions of free books, films, recordings and software, and it has public APIs. But turning "every Mark Twain audiobook, with MP3 links" into a clean table still means juggling two APIs, Solr query syntax, a 10,000-result paging limit and metadata that's sometimes a string and sometimes a list. I'm an 18-year-old engineering student, and I wrapped all of that in an actor called Internet Archive Scraper . This post shows how to call it from Python and Node, what the data looks like, and one small project: a public-domain reading list with direct EPUB links. How it works, briefly The actor calls archive.org's own search API ( advancedsearch.php ) and, if you ask for files, the metadata API ( /metadata/{identifier} ). No browser, no login. Plain-word searches are limited to title, subjects and creator by default, because archive.org's full-text search is very noisy: when I sorted "moby dick" by downloads over full text, the top hit was a 1948 film noir. With the default, the top hits are actual Moby-Dick editions. Python example pip install apify-client from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( " <YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN> " ) run = client . actor ( " rel8ble/internet-archive-scraper " ). call ( run_input = { " queries " : [ " apollo 11 " ], " mediaTypes " : [ " movies " ], " sortBy " : " downloads " , " maxResults " : 20 , }) for item in client . dataset ( run [ " defaultDatasetId " ]). iterate_items (): print ( item [ " title " ], item [ " year " ], item [ " downloads " ], item [ " url " ]) Node example npm install apify-client import { ApifyClient } from " apify-client " ; const client = new ApifyClient ({ token : " <YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN> " }); const run = await client . actor ( " rel8ble/internet-archive-scraper " ). call ({ queries : [ ' creator:"Mark Twain" ' ], mediaTypes : [ " audio " ], sortBy : " downloads " , maxResults : 50 , includeFiles : true , fileFormats : [ " mp3 " ], }); const { items } = await client . dataset ( run . defaultDatasetId ). listItems (); for ( const it of items ) console . log ( it . title , it . filesCount , " MP3 files " ); What comes back One item per archive.org item. This is a real row from a test run ("moby dick", sorted by downloads, file formats limited to PDF/EPUB), trimmed: { "query" : "moby dick" , "identifier" : "mobydickorwhale01melvuoft" , "title" : "Moby-Dick; or, The whale" , "mediaType" : "texts" , "creator" : "Melville, Herman, 1819-1891" , "year" : 1922 , "publisher" : "London Constable" , "collections" : [ "robarts" , "toronto" , "university_of_toronto" ], "downloads" : 135030 , "downloadsLastWeek" : 678 , "pageCount" : 398 , "url" : "https://archive.org/details/mobydickorwhale01melvuoft" , "filesCount" : 2 , "files" : [ { "name" : "mobydickorwhale01melvuoft.epub" , "format" : "EPUB" , "sizeBytes" : 1433807 , "url" : "https://archive.org/download/mobydickorwhale01melvuoft/mobydickorwhale01melvuoft.epub" } ] } You also get subjects, language, license URL, rights, favorites, ratings, runtime for video and audio, ISBNs and a thumbnail URL. One detail I cared about: archive.org lists users' personal favourite lists as fav-<username> collections, and the actor strips those out. Use case: a public-domain text corpus with direct links The goal: the 50 most downloaded English books in archive.org's Project Gutenberg collection, with a direct link to each plain-text file, saved as CSV. That's a small, clean corpus for NLP experiments or a reading list. import csv from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( " <YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN> " ) run = client . actor ( " rel8ble/internet-archive-scraper " ). call ( run_input = { " collection " : " gutenberg " , " mediaTypes " : [ " texts " ], " language " : " eng " , " sortBy " : " downloads " , " maxResults " : 50 , " includeFiles " : True , " fileFormats " : [ " txt " ], }) with open ( " gutenberg-top50.csv " , " w " , newline = "" , encoding = " utf-8 " ) as f : w = csv . writer ( f ) w . writerow ([ " title " , " creator " , " downloads " , " txt_url " , " bytes " ]) for it in client . dataset ( run [ " defaultDatasetId " ]). iterate_items (): txt = ( it . get ( " files " ) or [{}])[ 0 ] w . writerow ([ it [ " title " ], it . get ( " creator " ), it [ " downloads " ], txt . get ( " url " , "" ), txt . get ( " sizeBytes " , "" )]) In my test run, the top result was Amusements in Mathematics by Henry Ernest Dudeney (2,767,810 downloads), with its text at https://archive.org/download/amusementsinmath16713gut/16713-8.txt . queries is empty here on purpose: when you only set filters, the actor lists the whole collection. Swap gutenberg for prelinger (old films) or oldtimeradio and change the format filter to h.264 or mp3 . One thing I learned: Gutenberg items on archive.org carry text and HTML files, not EPUBs, and most have no year , so don't add a year filter to this one. What it costs Pricing is $1.00 per 1,000 results, and one result is one archive.org item, with or without its file list. The corpus above: 50 items = $0.05 A 1,000-item catalog of a collection = $1.00 Apify's free plan gives $5 of monthly credit, which covers about 5,000 items Limits These come straight from my testing: 10,000 results per query. archive.org's search API won't page further. Split by year or media type. File lists add one request per item. Audiobooks can have hundreds of files, so a 300-item run with files took about 5 minutes locally at concurrency 5. The default is now 10. Metadata is whatever the uploader entered. In a 300-item test, 78% had a date, 44% a license URL and 26% a publisher. It doesn't download files , it gives you the URLs. Check each item's license before reusing anything. One oddity I hit while building it: archive.org's newer "scrape" API cached responses and returned the same results for different queries. The actor uses the older, stable search API instead. If something breaks or a field is wrong, the Issues tab on the actor page reaches me directly. Internet Archive Scraper on Apify This article was drafted with AI and published by me.

title: How much GPU energy does fp16 save? Measured on a Tesla T4
author: bsharma173860-oss
summary: How much GPU energy does fp16 actually save over fp32? Spec sheets give TDP and peak FLOPS, not joules per job, so I measured it on a Tesla T4 using the GPU's own NVML energy counter. The job import sys , torch dtype = { " fp16 " : torch . float16 , " fp32 " : torch . float32 }[ sys . argv [ 1 ]] a = torch . randn ( 8192 , 8192 , device = " cuda " , dtype = dtype ) for _ in range ( 100 ): b = a @ a torch . cuda . synchronize () fp16 and fp32 runs alternate (so temperature and clock drift hit both sides), 5 measured runs each, medians reported, Mann-Whitney test between the two. Results: the whole job Setup fp16 fp32 GPU energy saved No cooling between runs 475 J, 8.6 s 2.53 kJ, 39.7 s 81.2% Every run starts at ≤65 °C 426 J, 7.8 s 2.21 kJ, 33.8 s 80.8% ≤65 °C + 3 warm-up runs 413 J, 8.4 s 2.50 kJ, 40.1 s 83.5% Same, a second session 392 J, 7.9 s 2.29 kJ, 36.1 s 82.9% p = 0.008 every time: every fp16 run beat every fp32 run. Results: just the matmuls Measuring inside the process, without Python start-up and CUDA set-up, 20 matmuls took about 73 J and 1.1 s in fp16 against about 486 J and 7.4 s in fp32: roughly 85% less GPU energy and 6.6× faster. import torch , joules with joules . Session ( gpus = [ 0 ]) as s : with s . phase ( " fp16 " ) as p : ... # your code print ( p . energy_j , p . duration_s ) Why the gap is so large The T4 is Turing: fp16 matmuls run on the tensor cores, but there is no TF32, so fp32 runs on the ordinary CUDA cores. Energy is power × time, so most of the saving comes from finishing sooner. fp32 also sat throttled 93% of the time at the T4's 70 W cap, against about 60% for fp16. On an A100, H100 or L4, fp32 matmuls can use TF32, so expect a much smaller gap there. Measure it rather than assume it. Run it yourself pip install -U landauer-gap joules compare --names fp16,fp32 --baseline fp32 --runs 5 --warmup 3 --cool-to 65 --gpus 0 \ "python3 bench.py fp16" "python3 bench.py fp32" Full write-up with power and throttling tables: https://wattops.dev/blog/fp16-vs-fp32-gpu-energy-t4 Disclosure: I built joules, the open-source CLI used here.

title: Why your AI agent gets fund holdings wrong: the SEC's "Ticker" field isn't a ticker
author: Alex B
summary: If you are building an agent or a model on SEC fund-holdings data, it will read a field called IDENTIFIER_TICKER and trust it. Here is what that field actually contains. If you build fund-ownership data from SEC Form N-PORT, you will read a field called IDENTIFIER_TICKER and treat it as a stock symbol. The SEC's data-set documentation describes it in one word: "Ticker". The form itself says more. Form N-PORT, Item C.1.e, asks for "at least one" other identifier: an ISIN, or a "Ticker (if ISIN is not available)", or some other identifier. Nothing requires the ticker to be an exchange symbol. It is a fallback. So we measured what funds actually put there - every quarter the SEC has published, 2019 Q4 to 2026 Q2: 17,361,050 rows carry a ticker. 72% are on common-stock lines, and they look like real tickers: MSFT, AMZN, AAPL. On mortgage-backed lines (676,336 rows) the "tickers" are agency pool-type prefixes: FN 161,550 rows, GN 109,156, FNMA 55,140, FHLMC 45,223. On bond lines (2,312,102 rows) the ticker is the ISSUER's stock symbol, not the bond's: AT&T bonds carry "T" on 86,298 rows. On derivative lines you find futures contract codes (TYZ2, ESZ2) and currency codes (USD, EUR). Why it matters: FG is a Freddie Mac pool prefix. It is also the NYSE ticker of F&G Annuities & Life. Join N-PORT's ticker field to a ticker list and Freddie Mac mortgage pools turn into holdings of an insurance company. Bond holdings turn into stock holdings. Ownership counts, "smart money" signals and flow features all inherit it - silently. Two more traps in the same files: Placeholders that look like data: ISSUER_CUSIP is "N/A" on 47.5 million rows, "000000000" on 15.2 million and "999999999" on 210 thousand. ISSUER_LEI is "N/A" on 67.6 million. Count those as filled and your coverage numbers are wrong. The SEC's machine-readable field list ships unchanged with every historical quarter, so a field "defined" there may not exist in older files (the VaR table is listed back to 2019 but only appears from 2022 Q1). What to do: before trusting any identifier on an N-PORT line, check what kind of holding the line is (the ASSET_CAT field), and treat placeholder values as blank. What I don't know yet: Whether anyone publishes an open mapping from N-PORT pool prefixes (FN, GN, FG...) to the agency programs they stand for. I could not find one. How much of the bond-line "issuer ticker" habit comes from filers themselves and how much from the software vendors that prepare their filings. We published the full N-PORT field dictionary - the SEC's definitions with citations, the official code lists, and what is actually in each field - free, under CC BY 4.0: https://alexbocio.github.io/us-gov-data-dictionary/sec_nport.html Source data: SEC Form N-PORT data sets, 2019 Q4 - 2026 Q2. If you build fund-ownership data from N-PORT: how do you handle the non-stock lines today - map them, or drop them? And if someone has already solved this better, link it in the comments and I'll credit it in the dictionary.

title: Hyperdocs: An AI Documentation Platform That Keeps Up With Your Product
author: Suriya Kumar
summary: Hyperdocs is an AI documentation platform for SaaS teams. It helps you create docs, keep them accurate, and see what’s missing. What you can publish Everything lives in one place: Product docs: guides, onboarding steps and feature pages Help center: articles where customers can find answers API docs: guides and endpoint references Changelog: release notes and product updates Three ways to get started You don’t have to start from code. Write: use the visual editor to build and organize articles. Generate: connect GitHub and get editable drafts based on your product and code. Migrate: import your existing docs, including from Mintlify, and keep refining them. Keeping docs current This is the hard part, and Hyperdocs has three tools for it: GitHub Sync: shows which pages may be affected after a code change. Docs Audit: finds missing and outdated documentation. You can run it manually or on a schedule. Docs Agent: drafts new pages, edits existing ones or fills gaps. Your team reviews every update before it goes live. Helping users find answers Answer Agent: answers visitors’ questions using your published docs and links them back to the source pages. Analytics: shows what people search for, which searches return nothing and what readers think of each page. Multilingual docs: translate and publish in more than one language. AI and SEO visibility: structured pages that search engines and AI tools can find and use. Your code stays under your control Hyperdocs connects to your repository with read-only access. Per the site, your code isn’t used to train AI models and repository secrets aren’t read. Who it’s for Product teams, technical writers, engineering teams and customer support teams, so everyone who owns the docs can work from the same place. Try it You can publish docs in minutes with no credit card. Start at hyperdocs.io.

title: GroundTruth OSINT: free live global monitoring — 170 feeds, 3D globe, daily brief, no signup
author: OSINT Watch
summary: A month ago I posted about a side project: a free live global monitoring dashboard. Since then it's been rebranded, rebuilt, and grown a lot. Here's where it stands. GroundTruth OSINT — https://groundtruthosint.com A free, no-signup dashboard that pulls 170 live reporting feeds — official sources (White House, combatant commands), major outlets, specialists — and correlates them into a single global picture on a 3D globe, refreshed every 15 minutes. The philosophy: detect, correlate, assess. Show what multiple sources report, label the source types, don't editorialize. Raw global awareness without the TV news spin. What's in it: Live 3D globe with 150 tracked events, clickable markers (sources, plain-language "So what," market-impact context) Ranked reports page with keyword + priority search and a triage queue Shareable deep links to any event — send someone straight to a story "New since your last visit" highlighting so you see what changed Optional layers: live wildfire data (NASA FIRMS), earthquakes (USGS M4.5+), severe weather Free daily morning brief — top events in your inbox at 6:30 AM ET, just an email, no account No signup, no paywall, works on mobile The stack: one Cloudflare Worker + D1. Feed polling, clustering, and priority scoring all happen server-side on a 15-minute cycle; the browser just renders. The globe is canvas-rendered with pre-baked marker sprites (learned the hard way that per-frame shadowBlur melts mobile GPUs). Snapshot-backed API took cold loads from 38s to ~1.5s. The honest part: it costs $5/month to run plus feed bandwidth. There's a small donation link on the site — that's the entire business model. The tool is free, no tiers, no gates. What's next: user-defined watch keywords (track your topics, not just the global picture), better source-diversity scoring. It's live: https://groundtruthosint.com — I'd genuinely love feedback from devs: what would you track that it doesn't? Any feeds I'm missing? Disclosure: the linked site has a small donation link that helps cover operating costs.

title: I Built SpeedPulse: An Open-Source Internet Speed Tester with ASP.NET Core 10 and TypeScript
author: Sanskar
summary: I Built SpeedPulse: An Open-Source Internet Speed Tester with ASP.NET Core 10 and TypeScript After working on its testing interface, diagnostics, backend, and release pipeline, I'm excited to introduce SpeedPulse v1.0.0 , the first stable release of my open-source internet speed testing project. SpeedPulse is designed to provide an approachable way to measure connection performance while giving developers additional tools to explore network behavior. What is SpeedPulse? SpeedPulse is a browser-based internet speed testing application. It provides measurements for download and upload throughput, HTTP latency, approximate jitter, and failed HTTP probes, alongside interactive charts and results history. You can try it directly on GitHub Pages: https://sanskarin.github.io/SpeedPulse/ Features in v1.0.0 1. Connection speed testing SpeedPulse provides: Download and upload speed measurements HTTP latency and approximate jitter Failed HTTP probe monitoring Live progress and visualizations These are browser-level estimates, rather than laboratory-grade or packet-level network measurements. 2. Interactive dashboard The application includes visualizations for exploring connection performance, along with locally stored results history. Users can export results as CSV and share their measurements. 3. Developer Labs One part of SpeedPulse that I'm particularly interested in developing further is Developer Labs. It brings together diagnostic utilities including backend health checks, HTTP probes, browser capability reporting, diagnostic exports, and explicitly labeled simulations. The goal is to make network behavior easier to inspect and understand. 4. Optional ASP.NET Core 10 backend SpeedPulse supports two deployment approaches. Hosted web version The GitHub Pages deployment uses a static frontend and public Cloudflare testing endpoints. Self-hosted version The optional ASP.NET Core 10 backend provides local HTTP testing endpoints, health and configuration APIs, bounded transfers, and request limiting. An important distinction: tests against a server running on the same computer measure the local loopback path, not your internet service provider's speed. Technology stack The project brings together: C# and ASP.NET Core 10 TypeScript and JavaScript HTML and CSS Chart.js Node.js build tooling GitHub Actions GitHub Pages Improving measurement reliability An important part of preparing v1.0.0 was improving how the application handles partial test failures. Previously, an upload failure could interrupt the experience even after earlier measurements had succeeded. The stable release now preserves completed measurements and marks an unavailable upload result appropriately instead of treating it as zero. I also corrected live chart behavior and added regression coverage for these scenarios. Download SpeedPulse v1.0.0 The release includes a static web archive and self-hosted ASP.NET Core packages for Windows x64, Linux x64, and Apple Silicon macOS. GitHub release: https://github.com/sanskarIN/SpeedPulse/releases/tag/v1.0.0 Source code: https://github.com/sanskarIN/SpeedPulse Live application: https://sanskarin.github.io/SpeedPulse/ What's next? Future development can continue improving measurement reliability, developer diagnostics, usability, and testing across different environments. Since the project is open source under the MIT License, contributions and technical feedback are welcome. If you explore SpeedPulse, I'd particularly love to hear about browser compatibility, unexpected measurement behavior, or ideas for making the diagnostics more useful. Thanks for checking out SpeedPulse! Built by Sanskar GitHub: https://github.com/sanskarIN Website: https://sanskarin.github.io

title: Building Cometflow Space: Designing Multi-Agent War Rooms for Autonomous Strategy & Execution
author: Pratyush Ranjan Roul
summary: Most AI interactions today rely on a single-prompt, single-bot paradigm. While this works well for simple scripts or generic summaries, real-world engineering, pricing overhauls, and product strategy require diverse perspectives and active debate. A single model prompt frequently suffers from confirmation bias, missing critical edge cases, operational bottlenecks, and financial trade-offs. To address these limitations, we designed Cometflow Space — an orchestration platform powered by 38+ always-active autonomous agents engineered to collaborate, challenge one another, and execute like an executive leadership team. The above image shows you the agents ! This image shows how we choose the role and responsibilities. The War Room! The Challenge: Single-Agent Limitations Standard generative interfaces introduce several bottlenecks when handling complex engineering and business workflows: Confirmation Bias: Single LLM threads often agree with user premises rather than pointing out foundational flaws. Siloed Competencies: Software architecture, pricing mechanics, and operational readiness are evaluated in isolation rather than together. Lack of Persistence: Traditional agents wait passively for user prompts instead of running continuous monitoring loops. Cometflow tackles this by deploying a persistent, multi-agent council with structured debate mechanics. Core System Architecture The Multi-Agent War Room (Cross-Bot Debate) The War Room serves as the operational center for high-stakes initiatives: Autonomous Cross-Critique: When a mission is triggered, agents do not merely answer questions; they critique each other's proposals, expose operational risks, and debate trade-offs. Structured Execution Phases: Discussions move systematically through phases (e.g., Phase 1/5: Objective & Positions), guiding teams from alignment to tactical roadmaps. Human-in-the-Loop Orchestration: As the executive lead (CEO), you can intervene directly, poll the entire room, or query specific domain leads (e.g., @chief of Staff, @Document Intelligence). Preset triggers like Challenge Pricing and Flag Backend Bottlenecks allow immediate redirection during live debates. AI Council Briefing Missions begin with structured domain parameters rather than open-ended, ambiguous prompts: Objective Formulation: Clearly define target initiatives, such as transitioning a platform from a flat subscription to a hybrid usage-based metering model. Domain Specialization: Select target niches (e.g., SaaS & Tech Startup, Fintech & Business Operations, EdTech, or E-Commerce) to load domain-specific personas, risk models, and operational frameworks. Always-On Autonomous Background Agents Beyond synchronous war rooms, Cometflow runs persistent background loops: Continuous Operations: Background agents run 24/7 loops. For example, Nexus-Dev monitors module dependencies and runs test validations, while the Chief of Staff synthesizes operational priorities across workspaces. Asset and Document Auditing: Specialized agents continuously crawl links, audit visual assets, and inspect documentation to keep system knowledge updated around the clock. War Room Execution Workflow [ Step 1: Define Mission & Domain Niche ] │ ▼ [ Step 2: Configure Bots & Council ] │ ▼ ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Autonomous War Room Debate │ │ - Cross-critique pricing & schemas │ │ - Identify backend choke points │ │ - Triage multi-disciplinary trade-offs│ └────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ [ Synthesized, Production-Ready Plan ] By structuring multi-agent handoffs, Cometflow eliminates the friction of manual role-prompting and turns agentic communication into an actionable consensus protocol. Key Takeaways Shifting from passive conversational AI to multi-agent war rooms changes how teams make mission-critical decisions. It bridges the gap between high-level architectural brainstorming and concrete operational execution. This article took me 1 hour to write specially the architecture and if you are exploring agentic architectures, how do you approach consensus and trade-off validation across autonomous LLMs? Share your thoughts and learnings below!

title: Add CSV imports to a React app with column mapping and validation
author: aimodels-fyi
summary: A CSV parser gives you rows. A customer-facing import feature needs a few more decisions: What if the customer's headers don't match your database fields? What if a required email address is missing? Can users correct mistakes without editing and uploading the file again? How do the finished records reach your backend? I built CSVJetty to handle that workflow. This tutorial shows how to add it to a React app and receive the imported records. What we're building A contact importer with three fields: First name: required Last name: optional Email: required and validated Users upload a CSV, review the column mappings, correct invalid values, and submit the records. We'll use callback delivery. CSVJetty processes the CSV in the browser and passes the imported rows to your application without routing row data through CSVJetty's servers. The service still receives import metadata. 1. Install the package npm install csvjetty Create an importer in the CSVJetty dashboard and select OnData Callback as its delivery mode. Copy its public importer key. The example below defines the columns in code. 2. Add the importer Create ImportContacts.jsx : " use client " ; import { useState } from " react " ; import CSVJetty from " csvjetty " ; const columns = [ { name : " first_name " , label : " First name " , type : " text " , required : true , aliases : [ " First Name " , " Given Name " ], }, { name : " last_name " , label : " Last name " , type : " text " , required : false , aliases : [ " Last Name " , " Surname " ], }, { name : " email " , label : " Email " , type : " email " , required : true , aliases : [ " Email Address " , " Work Email " ], }, ]; export default function ImportContacts () { const [ contacts , setContacts ] = useState ([]); return ( < section > < h1 > Import contacts </ h1 > < CSVJetty importerKey = "YOUR_IMPORTER_KEY" columns = { columns } onData = { async ({ rows }) => { setContacts ( rows ); } } > Import CSV </ CSVJetty > { contacts . length > 0 && ( < div > < h2 > Imported contacts: { contacts . length } </ h2 > < pre > { JSON . stringify ( contacts , null , 2 ) } </ pre > </ div > ) } </ section > ); } Replace YOUR_IMPORTER_KEY with your public importer key. This example displays the records in memory so you can inspect the output. It doesn't save them to a database. The "use client" directive allows this component to work in Next.js App Router. In a plain React app, you can omit it. 3. Try a file with different headers Save this as contacts.csv : Given Name,Surname,Work Email Ada,Lovelace,ada@example.com Grace,Hopper,grace@example.com Katherine,Johnson,not-an-email Upload the file using the Import CSV button. The aliases help match Given Name to first_name , Surname to last_name , and Work Email to email . Users can review and adjust the mappings. The third record contains an invalid email. Correct it to katherine@example.com in the preview before importing. In the dashboard, enable Disable Importing All Data if There Are Invalid Rows if you want to require every row to pass validation before submission. The callback receives records using your configured field names: [ { "first_name" : "Ada" , "last_name" : "Lovelace" , "email" : "ada@example.com" }, { "first_name" : "Grace" , "last_name" : "Hopper" , "email" : "grace@example.com" }, { "first_name" : "Katherine" , "last_name" : "Johnson" , "email" : "katherine@example.com" } ] Your backend gets a consistent shape even when customers use different CSV headers. 4. Connect your existing save endpoint Once the preview works, update ImportContacts.jsx to send the records to your application's API: " use client " ; import { useState } from " react " ; import CSVJetty from " csvjetty " ; const columns = [ { name : " first_name " , label : " First name " , type : " text " , required : true , aliases : [ " First Name " , " Given Name " ], }, { name : " last_name " , label : " Last name " , type : " text " , required : false , aliases : [ " Last Name " , " Surname " ], }, { name : " email " , label : " Email " , type : " email " , required : true , aliases : [ " Email Address " , " Work Email " ], }, ]; export default function ImportContacts () { const [ importedCount , setImportedCount ] = useState ( null ); async function handleImport ({ rows , importId , rowNumbers }) { const response = await fetch ( " /api/contacts/import " , { method : " POST " , headers : { " Content-Type " : " application/json " , }, body : JSON . stringify ({ rows , importId , rowNumbers , }), }); if ( ! response . ok ) { throw new Error ( " Could not save contacts. Please try again. " ); } setImportedCount ( rows . length ); } return ( < section > < h1 > Import contacts </ h1 > < CSVJetty importerKey = "YOUR_IMPORTER_KEY" columns = { columns } onData = { handleImport } > Import CSV </ CSVJetty > { importedCount !== null && ( < p role = "status" > Saved { importedCount } contacts. </ p > ) } </ section > ); } /api/contacts/import is an endpoint you implement in your own app. This example assumes a successful response means all submitted rows were saved. The endpoint should authenticate the user, check their permission to import contacts, validate the records again, and save them. Use importId and the original row numbers to prevent duplicate inserts when a request is retried. Browser validation helps users correct their files. Server validation protects your database. Where to go next The same pattern works for product catalogs, inventory, leads, and other structured records: define the fields, let users map and correct their data, then send the results to your existing persistence code. You can find the package and setup instructions here: CSVJetty website CSVJetty on npm

title: Playwright 1.64 adds WebMCP. What changes for your tests?
author: Anton Gulin
summary: Originally published on anton.qa . This release matters when your website offers actions for AI agents to call. WebMCP lets a page offer those actions. Playwright 1.64 adds experimental support for listing and calling them. If your website offers no WebMCP actions, there are none to test yet. If your team is adding them, you can check them alongside the normal page journey. Keep your normal browser tests. The extra checks concern what these website actions return and change. A delivery-date example Imagine your website offers AI an action to find an order's delivery date. A tool is the callable action your website provides. Suppose test order 1043 has a saved delivery date of October 16. Call the lookup with that order number. Compare the reply with the saved date, and confirm the records stayed unchanged. This is an illustrative example, not a recorded test run. Your website must register the action, and your browser needs WebMCP enabled. Start with a supported page and browser Your application must register tools through the browser's experimental WebMCP interface. The browser also needs WebMCP enabled. Chromium needs --enable-features=WebMCP when the browser starts. Firefox needs both dom.modelcontext.enabled and dom.modelcontext.testing.enabled preferences. WebKit does not implement the feature. The Playwright API calls the main frame's instance page.webmcp . A frame is one page area with its own content. A tool inside a child frame belongs to that frame's frame.webmcp instance. Choose the frame that actually registers the tool. These prerequisites matter before you diagnose a missing tool. A page without registered tools does not establish that your test setup failed. An empty list can be correct for a page without tools. List what the page offers tools() returns tools currently registered in the chosen frame. Compare the names with the actions your application intended to offer. Check the description and input shape too. An input schema describes the values a tool expects. The page supplies names, descriptions, input rules, and annotations, which are hints about behavior. Treat those page-provided details as untrusted input. An annotation saying an action is read-only is a page-provided hint. It does not prove the action cannot change data. If a tool is missing, first check the chosen frame and registration timing. Then check whether your application registered it. tools() can also throw when the browser lacks WebMCP support. Call one tool and check its effect callTool() invokes a named tool in the chosen frame. Select an action with a known expected result in your own application. Supply the input that matches its schema. The call returns the result supplied by the page's tool. Check both the returned content and the application result. For our order lookup, compare the reply with the known delivery date. For an update, read the saved record after the call. Check the intended change and confirm other records stayed unchanged. Follow the app's documented save timing. A returned value only tells you that the tool answered. It does not prove the answer is correct or the update persisted. Use a controlled record for actions that change data. Keep purchases and customer notifications outside this check. A callback is the code that runs the tool. Situation to exercise What Playwright exposes What the tester should check Valid tool and input The page's returned result Expected content and the relevant application state Tool returns isError: true A returned error result The reported failure and whether state stayed as expected Name is not registered An exception, a reported execution failure The intended registration and the reported failure Tool's callback throws An exception, a reported execution failure The reported failure and resulting application state The last two cases both fail through an exception. That failure alone does not identify its cause. Inspect the registered names and the controlled failure you exercised. Keep the normal page journey A page-tool check tells you what an AI-facing action reports and changes. It does not replace a person's normal browser journey. Keep tests for visible controls, messages, and the complete user task. Those checks answer a different question: can a person finish the task through the page? A short review list For your own tool-enabled page, ask: Which frame registers the tool, and is WebMCP enabled in this browser? Does tools() show the expected action and input shape? Does callTool() return the expected content for a known input? Does the application state match that result? What happens for a returned error, an unknown name, and a callback failure? Do normal page controls still support the user's task? That list gives you a practical starting point for Playwright 1.64. Adapt each expected result to your application's actual contract. I'm Anton. I build AI tools and measure how fast they really run. Former Apple engineer. I make ollamatps.com and write about building and measuring AI at anton.qa .

title: Google Photos + AI Storage Assistant
author: Naila Akram
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built You know that notification you get on your phone saying your storage is almost full? I get it every few days, and honestly, it's annoying. Whenever I see it, I open my gallery and start looking for photos I can delete. But then I find so many similar pictures, random screenshots, and photos I don't even remember saving. Sometimes I want to delete a photo, but I stop because I'm not sure if I'll need it later. And the worst part is figuring out which photos are duplicates. Going through hundreds of pictures one by one just to free up some space feels like too much work. That's where I got the idea for Google Photos + AI Storage Assistant . I wanted to build something that could make managing photos easier. The idea is to have a photo gallery where I can browse my pictures, organize them into albums, save my favorites, and eventually get help from AI when I need to clean up my storage. So far, I've built a Google Photos-inspired interface with a photo gallery, categories, favorites, an album suggestion interface, and an AI assistant. Here's what it currently has: A gallery to browse photos. Categories like Travel, Nature, and Screenshots. A favorites feature for important photos. A suggested album interface where users can select photos. An AI chat assistant that runs using a local AI model. A storage management section that I'm working to improve. It's still a prototype, and I know there's a lot more I want to add. Duplicate detection is one of the features I'd really like to build next because it would solve the exact problem that inspired this project. My idea is simple: I want cleaning up a photo gallery to take less time and feel less stressful. Demo 🎥 Demo video: https://youtu.be/8dFOMaO5un4 Code 💻 GitHub: Repository Link - https://github.com/nailaAkr/ai-storage-manager How I Built It I used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to build the frontend, and Node.js with Express for the backend. For the AI assistant, I used Ollama with the Llama 3.2 (1B) model . I wanted to try using an open-source model locally instead of relying on a paid AI API. Getting everything connected wasn't completely straightforward. I had to work through some issues with the backend and the AI model before I could get responses in my application. This project gave me a chance to learn by actually building something instead of just following tutorials. I also got to understand how a local AI model can be connected to a web application. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? I'm still learning, and I want to be able to experiment with AI without worrying about API costs every time I try something new. Using Ollama made that possible for this project. I could run the model on my own computer and experiment with integrating it into my application. I also like the idea of using open-source tools because they give developers the freedom to learn, experiment, and improve their projects. I'd like to explore more privacy-friendly features as I continue working on this, especially since photos can contain personal memories. What's Next? There are a few things I'd love to add: A way to find duplicate and similar photos. Suggestions for photos that users might want to review or delete. Search that lets users describe the photo they're looking for. Better album suggestions. More control over how personal photo data is handled. I know these features will take more work, but they're the direction I'd like to take the project in. My First User Right now, I'm building this around a problem I face myself, so I'd love to know if other people struggle with the same thing. Do you also get storage-full notifications all the time? How do you decide which photos to delete? And would you use an assistant that helps you find duplicates instead of checking everything manually? I'd love to hear your thoughts! Thanks for checking out my project. ❤️

title: We deleted the install step, and found out it was holding the whole design together
author: TuringCorp
summary: The first version of CloudPal had an install step. It was a small one, the kind you write in a week and stop thinking about. Deleting it took three weeks and changed more of the design than anything else we've done. This is the write-up of what that step was actually holding up, because "nothing to install" sounds like a packaging decision and turns out to be an architecture one. The machine is usually not yours The reason to delete it was embarrassingly ordinary. The people who need a document produced are frequently not sitting at their own computer. They're on a borrowed laptop, a work machine they don't administer, a hotel business centre, a partner's desk. And the task in front of them has a deadline attached to it, which is exactly the situation where you don't want to be making installation decisions. If you have ever hesitated in front of someone else's machine, you know the shape of the hesitation. It isn't really about disk space. It's that an install is a request for a piece of a computer that isn't yours, and every part of that request comes with a promise attached: a background process you now own, a permission you can't audit, an uninstall you'll have to remember on a day you'd rather not think about this at all. We could have made the installer quieter. Instead we asked what it was for, and the honest answer was: it was for our convenience, not the user's. So we took it out, and then spent the next three weeks finding out what had quietly grown around it. Once there's no local process, the tab can't own anything Here's the first thing that falls over. With an install, something keeps running on the machine after you close the window, and the mental model is comfortable: the work is local, the window is a view onto it. Remove the install and the browser tab becomes the only thing on the user's side — and a tab is a terrible owner of anything. It gets closed. It gets suspended when a laptop lid shuts. It gets duplicated. It reloads when it feels like it. So the run cannot live in the tab. That's not a preference, it's a constraint you either accept early or retrofit painfully. What follows from it is a short list of design decisions that stop being optional: The server has to be the only authority on what has happened. Not "the server syncs with the client". The client reports nothing it can't prove, and the record of a run comes from the side that was actually running it. Every request has to be safe to send twice. A tab that gets refreshed mid-flight will re-send things, and a person who isn't sure whether it worked will press the button again. If a retried request can produce a second copy of the output, you've built a product that punishes impatience, which is a large percentage of your users. Reconnection is a first-class state, not an error. The gap between "closed the laptop" and "opened it on the train" is not a failure mode to be apologised for. It's the normal path, and the interface owes the person a truthful account of what happened while they were gone. The uncomfortable part is that all three of those are cheap to say and expensive to hold. The tempting shortcut is to let the client cache the state and reconcile later, which works beautifully until two devices disagree, and then the merge logic becomes the product. An artifact can't live at a path The second thing that breaks is naming. On a machine, a document is a path: ~/Documents/brief-final-v2.docx . The path is the identity. It's also a lie that only holds while you stay on the same computer. Once the machine isn't in the loop, "where is it" cannot mean a folder. It has to mean something that survives a different device, a different browser, a cleared cache, a new job. In practice it has to be the account — which drags in the questions that path-based systems never had to answer, and that nobody enjoys: What happens to a document when someone edits it on a machine they'll never see again? If two people open the same thing and both change a paragraph, whose version is "the" version? When someone asks for the same thing next month, is that a new document, or a revision of the old one? Both are defensible. Only one can be the default. Our answer is deliberately boring: the thing you get is a document that lives in your account, with its own history, and it looks the same from any browser. Boring is the goal. An artifact that behaves differently depending on which machine you're holding is a support burden disguised as a feature. The permission dialog you never see Removing the installer removes the moment where the operating system asks the user to trust us. That's a real convenience, and it comes with an obligation that took us a while to state plainly. An install is also a permission grant. The app gets to touch the drive, read the folder it's pointed at, run in the background. We gave that up. So we don't have a foothold on the machine, and we must not behave as if we do — not in the copy, not in the product's implied promises, and not in the feature list we'd like to have. That's the reason CloudPal generates documents rather than tidying up the files you already have. It's not modesty, and it isn't a temporary state of affairs waiting on a roadmap. Reading someone's existing files requires precisely the local foothold we just deleted. Saying "no" to that feature is what makes "nothing to install" an actual claim instead of a slogan. You also deleted the settings dialog An install usually comes with somewhere to put configuration: a preferences pane, a project folder, a config file, a field for an API key. Take the install away and all of that goes with it. It sounds like a simplification. It is really a constraint. Because if there is no configuration surface, then everything the person needs to tell us has to fit in the sentence they type. That is a much harder bar than it looks. Asking someone to describe what they want is a fine interface for a person who already knows; it is a poor one for the far more common case, where they know what the finished thing should look like and have no vocabulary for the steps in between. With a settings pane you hand them a form and let the form do the thinking. Without one, the product has to do the thinking — and it has to be willing to ask, briefly, once or twice, inside the same conversation rather than in a wizard nobody finishes. So we ended up with an internal rule that is more useful than it sounds: any feature that can only be configured by adding a field to a form is a feature we haven't finished. It either fits in the conversation or it doesn't ship yet. This is why the first thing CloudPal gives you is a result rather than a setup screen. Not for the demo's sake — because we ran out of places to hide the configuration. What we gave up It would be dishonest to present this as a clean win. Three things got worse, and they're worth naming because a developer reading this will think of them anyway. Local speed. Work that could have used a fast local machine and an existing local corpus now has to be produced on our machines from what was said in the conversation. That is a real ceiling. Offline. No install, no local runtime, no work on a plane with no wifi. The connection is the product. Private context. If your material lives somewhere you can't paste, this is the wrong tool for that job today. We'd rather say that than imply otherwise and disappoint someone at the end of a deadline. Those are the costs. What you buy for them is that the thing works on the machine you happen to be in front of, and that leaving is free — close the tab and there is nothing of ours left on that computer, because there was never anything there. A test that takes five minutes This is easy to check, which is why I like it. Use a computer that isn't yours, or a browser profile you don't care about. Open CloudPal, sign in, ask for something real, and then close the window before it's finished. Come back later on a different machine and see whether the thing you asked for is where you left it and says what actually happened. If that works, you've learned something more useful than any feature list: the work wasn't happening in the window, and the result doesn't belong to the computer. What we do about it CloudPal runs long tasks on our machines, on a schedule if you want one, and hands back a finished document — nothing to install, nothing asked of your computer, nothing read from files you already have. You say what you want and when you want it, in a sentence, and the output is a document you can forward rather than an answer you have to reassemble. It's in limited preview. New accounts get a dollar of credit, which is enough to run something real, and the number of new accounts per day is capped. If you want to judge it as an engineer, the question I'd put to it isn't whether it's clever. It's this: close the tab mid-run, then go find out whether it can tell you what it did while you weren't looking. An agent that only exists while you're watching is a chat window with extra steps. CloudPal.TuringCorp.net — create an Agent Pass, sign in, and say what you want done. Earlier in this series: what breaks when an agent has to keep an appointment .

title: How to Generate MiniMax H3 RH Enhanced Videos via API: Text, Frames and Multi-Reference, With Polling or a Webhook
author: Super Lewis
summary: A four-second 1080P clip from MiniMax H3 RH Enhanced took 218 seconds in our test. If your code holds an HTTP request open until the video exists, it will time out long before the video does. And because one model id covers three input modes, mixing the wrong fields gets you a 400 before anything renders. This tutorial shows the full loop for MiniMax H3 RH Enhanced: create a task, wait for it with polling or a webhook, download the MP4, verify it, and confirm what you were billed. MiniMax H3 RH Enhanced is an enhanced build of MiniMax's open-weight H3 video model that generates 4-to-15-second clips with an audio track at 480P, 768P or 1080P, from text, from a first and/or last frame, or from up to 9 reference images and 3 reference videos, optionally driven by your own audio. Disclosure: I work on apimodels.app, the API used in every example below, and the timings come from its test logs. I wrote this with AI assistance (DEV's "AI-Assisted" tier): the structure and prose were drafted with an AI, the request fields and error messages were checked against the API source, and the code is example code written against the documented contract. What you need Python 3.10+ and requests ( pip install requests ); Flask only if you want the webhook in Step 4. curl and, for verification, ffprobe from FFmpeg. An API key in an environment variable: export APIMODELS_KEY="sk_your_key_here" . Media as public HTTPS URLs. Images can also be sent as base64. For webhooks: a publicly reachable HTTPS URL. A tunnel such as ngrok works for local development; localhost and private addresses are rejected. Why one model id behaves like three The mode is picked from the fields you send, in this order: Any of reference_image_urls , reference_video_urls or reference_video_audio_urls → multi-reference . Otherwise, first_frame_url , last_frame_url or reference_audio_urls (voice references) → image-to-video . Otherwise → text-to-video , and prompt is required. Frames and references live in different pipelines, so a request with both is rejected at create time rather than having half its inputs silently ignored. Every mode also accepts audio_url (a driving track for lip sync) and audio_mode . The fields you will use most: Field Required Values model yes minimax-h3-rh-enhanced prompt text-to-video up to 20,000 characters duration yes 4–15 (seconds; billed for this number) resolution no 480p , 768p , 1080p ( default 1080p ) aspect_ratio no 1:1 2:3 3:2 3:4 4:3 9:16 16:9 21:9 first_frame_url , last_frame_url no URL or base64 reference_image_urls no up to 9 reference_video_urls no up to 3 reference_video_audio_urls no up to 2 (audio of the reference videos) audio_url no driving audio for lip sync reference_audio_urls no up to 3 voice references audio_mode no native (default), lock_source , remix_source , reference_only callback_url no public URL we POST the result to Step 1: Create a text-to-video task Start at 480P and 4 seconds while you test; it is the fastest and smallest combination. curl -s https://api.apimodels.app/v1/video/generations \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $APIMODELS_KEY " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "minimax-h3-rh-enhanced", "prompt": "A potter shapes a clay bowl on a spinning wheel, she looks up and smiles at the camera, warm window light", "duration": 4, "resolution": "480p", "aspect_ratio": "16:9" }' The response comes back immediately with a task ID and state: "pending" : { "code" : 200 , "msg" : "success" , "data" :{ "taskId" : "<task_id>" , "state" : "pending" , "model" : "minimax-h3-rh-enhanced" }} Step 2: Wait by polling The status endpoint returns state as pending , processing , completed or failed . On completed you get resultUrls ; on failed you get failMsg and a retryable flag. Poll every 10 to 15 seconds. # h3e.py — example client import json , os , time , requests BASE = " https://api.apimodels.app/v1 " HEADERS = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { os . environ [ ' APIMODELS_KEY ' ] } " } def create ( payload : dict ) -> str : r = requests . post ( f " { BASE } /video/generations " , headers = HEADERS , json = payload , timeout = 60 ) body = r . json () if r . status_code != 200 : raise RuntimeError ( f " { r . status_code } : { body . get ( ' msg ' ) } " ) return body [ " data " ][ " taskId " ] def wait ( task_id : str , every : int = 15 , give_up_after : int = 1800 ) -> dict : deadline = time . time () + give_up_after while time . time () < deadline : r = requests . get ( f " { BASE } /video/generations " , headers = HEADERS , params = { " task_id " : task_id }, timeout = 30 ) data = r . json ()[ " data " ] if data [ " state " ] == " completed " : return data if data [ " state " ] == " failed " : raise RuntimeError ( f " failed: { data . get ( ' failMsg ' ) } (retryable= { data . get ( ' retryable ' ) } ) " ) time . sleep ( every ) raise TimeoutError ( f " { task_id } still running after { give_up_after } s " ) Step 3: Download the result Result URLs point to MP4 files that are deleted after 30 days, so copy them to your own storage. def download ( url : str , path : str ) -> None : with requests . get ( url , stream = True , timeout = 300 ) as r : r . raise_for_status () with open ( path , " wb " ) as f : for chunk in r . iter_content ( 1 << 20 ): f . write ( chunk ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : task_id = create ({ " model " : " minimax-h3-rh-enhanced " , " prompt " : " A potter shapes a clay bowl on a spinning wheel, she looks up and smiles at the camera " , " duration " : 4 , " resolution " : " 480p " , " aspect_ratio " : " 16:9 " , }) print ( " task " , task_id ) data = wait ( task_id ) download ( data [ " resultUrls " ][ 0 ], f " { task_id } .mp4 " ) print ( " saved " , f " { task_id } .mp4 " , " billed USD: " , data [ " credits " ]) Step 4: Or let the API call you Add callback_url to the create body and the API POSTs to it when the task finishes, successful or not. The result URLs sit inside resultJson , which is a JSON string , so parse it. Return a 2xx quickly: each delivery attempt times out after 10 seconds and is tried up to three times. # webhook.py — example receiver (Flask) import json from flask import Flask , request app = Flask ( __name__ ) @app.post ( " /apimodels/callback " ) def callback (): data = request . get_json ( force = True )[ " data " ] urls = json . loads ( data . get ( " resultJson " ) or " {} " ). get ( " resultUrls " , []) print ( data [ " taskId " ], data [ " state " ], urls , data . get ( " credits " ), data . get ( " failMsg " )) # enqueue the download here; don't do slow work inside the request return "" , 200 Keep polling as a backstop for the rare callback your server misses. Step 5: Image-to-video with a driving audio track Same client, different body. A first frame plus a voice line turns a still portrait into a speaking shot. In our end-to-end test this exact shape at 480P and 4 seconds finished in 50 seconds. task_id = create ({ " model " : " minimax-h3-rh-enhanced " , " prompt " : " She keeps working and talks to the camera with a warm smile " , " first_frame_url " : " https://example.com/first.jpg " , " audio_url " : " https://example.com/voice.mp3 " , " duration " : 6 , " resolution " : " 480p " , " aspect_ratio " : " 3:4 " , }) Step 6: Multi-reference with your soundtrack locked Reference images set who and where, a reference video sets the movement, and audio_mode: "lock_source" keeps your song untouched. This is the slowest shape: a 6.6-second reference video pushed a 4-second 480P test to 346 seconds, so it is a good place to use the webhook. task_id = create ({ " model " : " minimax-h3-rh-enhanced " , " prompt " : " The singer from image 1 performs on the stage from image 2, moving like the dancer in the reference video " , " reference_image_urls " : [ " https://example.com/singer.jpg " , " https://example.com/stage.jpg " ], " reference_video_urls " : [ " https://example.com/dance.mp4 " ], " audio_url " : " https://example.com/song.mp3 " , " audio_mode " : " lock_source " , " duration " : 10 , " resolution " : " 768p " , " aspect_ratio " : " 9:16 " , " callback_url " : " https://your-app.example.com/apimodels/callback " , }) Verify it works Check the file's streams and length: ffprobe -v error -show_entries stream = codec_type,width,height,r_frame_rate:format = duration \ -of default = noprint_wrappers = 1 <task_id>.mp4 What our 2026-10-10 tests produced, so you know what "correct" looks like: a video stream at 24 fps plus an audio stream; 864×480 for 480P at 16:9, 544×768 for 480P at 3:4, 1920×1088 for 1080P at 16:9; and a duration about 0.46 seconds longer than requested. Then confirm the charge for that one task: curl -s https://api.apimodels.app/v1/records/<task_id> -H "Authorization: Bearer $APIMODELS_KEY " data.settled is true once the amount is final and data.credits is the USD taken from your balance, for example 0.2 for 480P × 4 seconds before any account discount, and 0 for a failed task. Where apimodels.app fits apimodels.app is a multi-model API gateway: one API key and one OpenAI-compatible endpoint for more than 140 image, video, audio and language models. For most mainstream models it keeps more than one upstream route with automatic failover; failed requests are not charged; long jobs run asynchronously with the webhook shown above; and GET /v1/records/{id} returns the exact charge for any single request. This model does not have a failover route yet: a failed job is refunded, and resubmitting is up to you (check retryable ). Pricing for minimax-h3-rh-enhanced is per requested second: $0.05 at 480P, $0.07 at 768P and $0.10 at 1080P. Reference images, reference videos and audio inputs are free. The MiniMax H3 RH Enhanced API reference lists every field and alias. Do not use it if you need a 1080P clip back in under a minute, need 2K or 4K, need clips longer than 15 seconds, or need a guaranteed native 1080P master: we have not verified whether 768P and 1080P are rendered natively or upscaled. Common errors All of these come back as HTTP 400 at create time. No task is created and nothing is charged. duration is required (4-15 seconds) : there is no default length. Send duration . duration must be between 4 and 15 seconds (got "20") : split longer scenes into several clips. prompt is required for text-to-video (or pass first_frame_url / reference_image_urls) : an empty prompt with no frames or references. first_frame_url / last_frame_url cannot be combined with reference_image_urls / reference_video_urls — use one mode per request : choose frames or references for each shot. resolution must be one of 480p / 768p / 1080p (got "720p") : there is no 720p tier. aspect_ratio must be one of 1:1 / 2:3 / 3:2 / 3:4 / 4:3 / 9:16 / 16:9 / 21:9 (got "5:4") . at most 9 reference images allowed (got 10) : the same pattern applies to 3 videos, 3 voice references and 2 reference-video audio tracks. callback_url host "localhost" is not reachable from our servers … : use a public URL or a tunnel. One failure arrives later, through failMsg : Content did not pass the safety review. Please change the reference media or prompt and try again. It is not charged. Limits Resolution tops out at 1080P, and the 1080P file is 1920×1088, not 1920×1080. Crop if your pipeline is strict. Omitting resolution renders at 1080P, the most expensive and slowest tier. The image-to-video and multi-reference timings above come from a handful of our own tests. We have not measured lip-sync accuracy or voice similarity. What turnaround time does your current video pipeline assume, and would a 218-second wait for a four-second 1080P clip break it? I build apimodels.app, one API key for 140+ image, video, audio and language models.

title: My OG image generator served a blank PNG to 40% of Slack previews — the cache key was the URL, not the title
author: InApp
summary: I built an OG image API that takes a title + description and renders a 1200x630 card. It worked great in my tests. Then I wired it into a link-unfurling pipeline for an agent that posts dozens of links into Slack channels, and suddenly a third of the previews came back gray. The bug wasn't in the renderer. It was in the CDN I put in front of it. Every generated image URL looked like /og?title=...&desc=... . The CDN cached on the full URL, which is correct — except Slack's unfurling bot strips query strings before requesting the image in some clients. So ?title=Deploy+failed and ?title=Deploy+succeeded both collapsed to /og/ , and the first response got cached for everyone else. One "Deploy failed" card got served to a channel full of "Deploy succeeded" links. The fix was boring and effective: hash the full parameter set into the path itself ( /og/a3f9c2….png ) and make the query string optional. Cache key and content now agree. What I actually learned: generated-image APIs are only as correct as the caching layer in front of them, and "the URL is the cache key" is a habit worth auditing whenever the URL's parameters carry the content . Agents building link previews, unfurlers, or card generators on top of an image API — check what your CDN sees, not just what you send. It's packaged here if you want to poke at it: https://x402.freeq.one/tools/og_image_generator.html The blank-card bug taught me more about HTTP caching than any blog post.
